clue.text: Old church with concerning orange-brown colour

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
CH is the usual abbreviation for church
re means about or concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: An ancient church painted in a warm orange-brown shade.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short crossword abbreviations line up in clue order; 'concerning' as RE is the one newcomers most often miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy pigment whose typical shade is a yellowish or reddish brown.

clue.text: Theoretically, Pope ran complex

indicators.note: something complex is intricate and tangled, so the letters are knotted into a new order

parts.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: In theory, the Pope was in charge of a whole complex of buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' reads as a noun the Pope ran, but it is an adjective telling you to scramble the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something true on paper holds in principle or in written plans, though perhaps not in practice.

clue.text: Priest at Eton is doing this in residential area

parts.words: Priest at Eton is doing this
parts.note: surface reading: a clergyman at the famous school is busy with some activity
setter's reading: these three words hold a six-letter word for land within their letters, so they are sheltering it

explanation.surface: A clergyman at Eton, the famous English boarding school, does something in a residential neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes itself: the words 'priest at Eton' literally contain ESTATE, so they are housing it. Eton is an elite English school.
explanation.definitionFit: A housing estate is a planned group of homes built together, a neighbourhood made up mostly of dwellings.

clue.text: Meet none cuter when travelling

indicators.note: things that travel move about from place to place, so the letters shift around

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller remarks that they never meet anyone more charming than on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meet' sits at the front looking like part of a sentence, but it is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To encounter someone is to come across or run into them, often unexpectedly.

clue.text: Dignity of former PM accepting joke

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece is received inside the other

parts.note: Theresa May was a British Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019
a jest is a joke

explanation.surface: A one-time prime minister keeps their dignity while taking a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Theresa May, British Prime Minister 2016-19, is the former PM; 'accepting' splits her name to admit the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Majesty is stately grandeur or impressive bearing, the regal quality of commanding respect.

clue.text: Unassuming way of working with stone

parts.note: a mode is a manner or method of operating
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A humble craft: someone quietly working stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working with stone' wants to be masonry, but the phrase splits after 'working'. A stone is a British unit of body weight, 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a person who does not boast or put themselves forward.

clue.text: He was patient and doctor?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Old Testament figure proverbial for enduring suffering

definitions.note: the verb 'doctor' fits the sense of crooked handling, as a put-up job
definitions.meaning: second meaning: to tamper with or fix dishonestly, as in a put-up piece of work

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs a patient with a doctor in a surgery; in fact 'patient' means long-suffering, and 'doctor' is a verb for rigging something.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical figure is famous for steadfast endurance, and a crooked arrangement or fix is also called by this word.

clue.text: Rate the setter "terrible" in performative displays?

definitions.note: plural phrase for a mass noun

indicators.note: something terrible is in a dreadful state, so the letters end up badly jumbled

parts.note: all thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A solver is invited to score the puzzle's compiler as awful at putting on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'terrible' look like the rating itself, but it is the anagram signal for the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Street theatre means performances staged in public outdoor places, shows put on for passers-by.

clue.text: Fluctuate rapidly, and ultimately say to boy: "No!"

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Someone sways back and forth, then finally tells a lad no.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted 'No!' feels like dialogue, but it is just the fourth word supplying a last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To yo-yo is to swing repeatedly up and down, like the spinning toy on a string.

clue.text: Swooped, once DUP fragmented

indicators.note: something fragmented has broken into bits, which can be put back in another order

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Rivals swooped once Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party split apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP is a Northern Irish political party, but here its letters are just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To pounce is to spring suddenly onto prey, exactly the motion of a bird diving down.

clue.text: Foolish British host

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a host is a great multitude, especially an army

explanation.surface: A silly British person throwing a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' suggests someone entertaining guests; its older sense is a vast army, as in 'heavenly host'.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is British slang for crazy or silly, a mild way of calling someone daft.

clue.text: Some VIP and Truss shifting portable gas cookers

indicators.note: shifting things move position, so the letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: letters taken as written
letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A dignitary and Liz Truss, a short-lived British Prime Minister, move some camping stoves around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' looks like a selection signal for a hidden word, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Primus is a brand of compact fuel-burning burner used for camping, so the plural names small carried cooking devices.

clue.text: Working actor not going topless immediately

indicators.note: going topless means losing what is on top, so the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a machine that is on is running or working
thesp is short for thespian, an actor
the word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A working actor refuses to take their top off on set.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a nudity clause in an acting contract; the words split into three small pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on the spot means doing it at once, right there and without delay.

clue.text: I agree south coast resort has no banks

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its two edges, so both outer letters are removed

parts.note: Brighton is a seaside town on England's south coast

explanation.surface: Someone concedes that a seaside town lacks any banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' suggests financial institutions; here they are the edges of the word, so the B and N go.
explanation.definitionFit: Righto is a casual British interjection meaning okay or all right, said when consenting.

clue.text: Still, tact is unusual

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters are put in a non-standard order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wry remark that diplomacy remains rare, even now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as the adverb 'even so'; it is the definition, as the adjective 'motionless'. 'Is' does double duty in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something static is not moving or changing, motionless and stationary.

clue.text: Camp erotic dancing back in vogue

indicators.note: dancers move their feet around, so these letters are moved about

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Flamboyant, suggestive dancing is fashionable again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' looks like an adjective for theatrical style, but it is the noun meaning a faction or clique.
explanation.definitionFit: A coterie is a small exclusive group sharing interests, just as rival camps are opposing groups of supporters.

clue.text: A new combination of notes cut short TV presenter

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
a chord is several notes sounded together

explanation.surface: A fresh blend of jingles sounds clipped when a television host speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Combination' tempts you to anagram, but it is part of the definition of a musical chord.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchor is the main host of a news broadcast, the person who links the reports together.

clue.text: Removal of odd chaps interrupting alien visitor briefly

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: ET, the film's extra-terrestrial, is short for an alien
odd means strange and chaps are men

explanation.surface: Peculiar men cut into a short visit from an extraterrestrial and take it away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' shortens the alien to its familiar two-letter film name; the odd chaps go between those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Estrangement is the state of being distanced or cut off from others, a kind of separation or withdrawal.

clue.text: Heterosexuality restricts love god

indicators.note: to restrict is to confine, so the longer word confines a shorter one within it

parts.note: the letters sit inside, after the first three

explanation.surface: Straight attraction alone limits the god of love.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits fittingly inside a word about desire.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of desire, counterpart of the Roman Cupid.

clue.text: Hand deliver a sermon, with no pressure

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so the named letter is taken away

parts.note: preaching is delivering a sermon
P is the symbol for pressure in physics

explanation.surface: A minister hand-delivers a sermon gently, without forcing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand deliver' looks like one compound verb; 'Hand' is the definition and the rest is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To hand someone something is to pass it over, and 'reach me that' is an older way to ask for it to be passed.

clue.text: Bore sheltered from sunlight, naked

indicators.note: naked means stripped of covering, so the outer letters come off

parts.note: a shady spot is out of the sun

explanation.surface: A dull person hid from the sun while unclothed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a noun for a tedious person; it is the past tense of bear, as in bore a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Bore and had both work as past tenses for giving birth to offspring, as in she bore or had twins.

clue.text: Bohemian joints — they're regularly ignored

parts.note: hips are joints of the body

indicators.note: ignoring at regular intervals means every other letter is skipped

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters are kept

explanation.surface: Bohemian cannabis joints, which people routinely overlook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joints' with 'Bohemian' suggests something smoked, but it means body joints; the apostrophe in the second word is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A bohemian is an unconventional, artistic person, which is what a trendy counterculture follower is.

clue.text: Meagre poster about Liberal

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: someone who posts a letter sends it
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A thin election placard about the Liberal candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poster' suggests a printed notice; it is a person who mails something.
explanation.definitionFit: Meagre and slender both describe a small or scanty amount, as in slender means or meagre resources.

clue.text: Article about that place

parts.note: the definite article
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a particular location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' usually signals a container or reversal; here it simply supplies RE.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb points to a location away from the speaker, exactly what the phrase names as a noun.
